name: Ajino Sanpei (originator shop of Sapporo miso ramen)
text: Sapporo shop regarded as the originator of miso ramen; founder-owner Omiya Morito. Sources differ on dating: one shop account says he conceived a miso-flavoured noodle bowl in 1955 with miso soup as the hint and put it on the menu in 1963, while Ramen Japan puts the trial of miso flavouring around 1954-1955. Nishiyama Seimen is named as the noodle maker that cooperated in development.
flavor: Miso-forward soup over curly yellow noodles; the shop's noodle is described as having its own colour from strong flour with no colouring added.
use: Pilgrimage shop for judging the baseline of Sapporo miso ramen against modern, lard-heavy versions.
craft: When citing the origin, give both dates (1955 trial, 1963 menu listing) and note the 1954-55 variant; the sources do not agree. The pairing of a maker-developed noodle with the miso soup is the point to study: noodle and tare were developed together.

name: Sapporo curly aged high-hydration noodle (Nishiyama Seimen type)
ja: 札幌ラーメンの熟成多加水縮れ麺(西山製麺)
text: The standard Sapporo ramen noodle is described as a curly, aged, high-hydration (tasui) noodle developed by Nishiyama Seimen, which cooperated in the development of miso ramen. It is characterised as chewy with strong elasticity and stickiness. Sources reviewed give no hydration percentage, thickness number or ageing time, so none is stated here.
flavor: Chewy, springy, with strong stickiness; yellow colour from flour and kansui.
use: Built to hold up in thick, oily miso soup; ordered to be eaten quickly at the counter.
craft: The curl and hydration are what let the noodle stand against heavy miso soup and a lard layer. Ask the supplier for exact hydration (kasui-ritsu) and ageing period, as the public sources do not give them.
src: Inojimania: Nishiyama Seimen souvenir miso ramen

name: Asahikawa Hachiya (burnt-lard shoyu ramen)
ja: 旭川ラーメン 蜂屋
text: Hachiya is named with Aoba as one of the two long-established shops of Asahikawa ramen. Asahikawa shoyu ramen is described as a double soup of seafood with pork bone and chicken bones, with low-hydration curly noodles and extra lard added to keep the soup hot. Hachiya's shoyu ramen is noted for burnt (kogashi) lard, and its soup colour is dark.
flavor: Dark, aromatic soup from burnt lard over a seafood-pork-chicken double base; hot to the end.
use: Reference shop for the Asahikawa lard-capped, hot-soup style, suited to cold climates.
craft: The lard layer acts as a lid to retain heat; the burning of the lard is the shop's signature, so judge by aroma and colour as much as by saltiness. Low-hydration noodle is the contrast to Sapporo's high-hydration style.

name: Kushiro ramen (clear shoyu with fine curly noodles)
text: Kushiro ramen is described as a clear shoyu ramen with fine curly noodles, the noodle being thinner than in other regions. Sources reviewed describe it as originating in Kushiro; they do not give a founding shop, year or hydration figure.
flavor: Clear, soy-based soup with a light body; fine, curled noodle.
use: Eaten as the fourth of Hokkaido's regional ramen alongside Sapporo, Hakodate and Asahikawa.
craft: Fine curly noodles cook fast and release starch quickly into clear soup; watch boil time and soup turbidity. Details of tare and oil are not given in the sources consulted.

name: Muroran curry ramen
text: Curry-flavoured ramen popular around Muroran, served with yellow curly noodles similar to Sapporo style. Origin accounts differ: most general sites say the 1960s in Muroran, an industrial steel and shipbuilding town; ramen21.jp says it spread from Iwamizawa to Muroran and Tomakomai via the Daio-style bowl; a note.com article places its birth in Tomakomai. The municipality promoted it as town revitalisation, and a Muroran Curry Ramen society was founded in 2006.
flavor: Curry-spiced soup over curly yellow noodles.
use: Local specialty; often eaten at the Daio-lineage shops.
craft: Because the origin is disputed, state the competing accounts rather than a single founder. Curry spice must be balanced against the base broth rather than overwhelming it; the sources give no recipe ratios.

name: Ajino Daio (Muroran curry ramen shop)
text: Curry ramen shop whose style is regarded in one source as the prototype of the curry ramen that spread in Muroran and Tomakomai. A note.com article says Daio opened in Muroran through a 1970s noren-wake, which helped the dish take root. In 1999 a former pop-group member recommended its curry ramen on radio, which made it a topic; the dish later became established through municipal promotion.
flavor: Curry-flavoured soup, local comfort food.
use: Benchmark for Muroran curry ramen.
craft: Sources conflict on whether the dish was born in Muroran or Tomakomai, and the Daio founding year is not given. Cite both accounts.

name: Akayu ramen (Nanyo, miso with karamiso topping)
text: Regional ramen of Nanyo, Yamagata. Described as a miso-based soup with thick curly noodles, topped with karamiso (chili miso) placed on top rather than mixed in. The topping is a red miso with chili and garlic and is said to have been completed in 1960. Ryujoukai is credited as origin.
flavor: Miso soup with growing heat as the chili miso is dissolved; thick curly noodle.
use: Karamiso is stirred in progressively to adjust spice.
craft: Keep the karamiso separate on the plate so the diner controls dilution; it is a topping, not part of the base tare.
src: Wikipedia JA: 赤湯ラーメン

name: Ryujoukai (Akayu karamiso ramen)
text: Shop in Akayu founded in 1958 (Showa 33). Wikipedia states the karamiso was completed in 1960 as chili and garlic added to red miso, served on top and not mixed into the soup. A source says the idea came from using left-over soup at home as miso soup. Nippon Ramen FC's Gotouchi Ramen Soran calls it the first shop to serve miso ramen in Tohoku.
flavor: Miso soup with a chili-garlic red miso on top.
use: Reference for Akayu ramen; karamiso ramen is also sold as take-home sets.
craft: The karamiso is not part of the stock; keep it as an add-on. The founding year of 1958 and karamiso year of 1960 come from separate sources.
src: Wikipedia JA: 赤湯ラーメン

name: Sakaeya Honten (Yamagata hiyashi ramen shop)
text: Yamagata shop known as the origin of hiyashi (cold) ramen, a bowl served with ice in the soup, available year-round. A restaurant roundup states the shop opened in Showa 7 (1932); the year when the cold bowl was first made is not given in the results reviewed here.
flavor: Icy, clean, with cold-chilled bite to the noodle.
use: Eaten year-round, not only in summer.
craft: Cold service demands shocking the noodles in ice water and a soup seasoned stronger than a hot version, since ice dilutes it.

name: Jumonji ramen (Yokote, Akita)
text: Local ramen of Yokote (former Jumonji town), Akita. Described as a light Japanese-style shoyu ramen with soup based on niboshi and katsuobushi, and thin curly noodles made without kansui.
flavor: Light, fish-based soup; soft thin curly noodle.
use: Local everyday ramen of southern Akita.
craft: Kansui-free noodle behaves differently from standard ramen noodle: pale colour, and it must be cooked and served with care so it does not go soft. Check dashi extraction time for niboshi bitterness.
src: Wikipedia JA category: Tohoku regional ramen

name: Shirakawa ramen
text: Fukushima regional ramen with a pork-bone and chicken-bone shoyu soup, described as stronger in soy than Kitakata ramen. The noodle is a wide, curled, high-hydration noodle that is hand-kneaded to give the curl.
flavor: Stronger shoyu than Kitakata; chewy wide noodle.
use: Local shoyu ramen of Shirakawa.
craft: Hand-kneading (temomi) gives irregular curl; hydration figures are not given in the sources.

name: Genraiken (Kitakata founding shop)
text: Shop regarded as the originator of Kitakata ramen. Its founder was Ban Kinsei, a Chinese man who came to Japan in the late Taisho era. One source dates the opening to Showa 1 (1926); other accounts describe it as beginning as a street stall, so the date is presented differently across sources. The shop's wonton is hand-pressed on green bamboo like its noodles.
flavor: Soy-based soup; hand-pressed noodle and wonton.
use: Wonton noodles are a speciality.
craft: Cite the founding date with caveat; the green-bamboo (aotake) hand-pressing is cited for the wonton and noodle.

name: Kitakata flat aged high-hydration noodle
ja: 喜多方 平打ち熟成多加水麺
text: The signature noodle of Kitakata is a flat (hirauchi), aged, high-hydration curly noodle; the dough is given plenty of water and then rested. The soup is shoyu-based, from niboshi and pork bone, using soy sauce from the local brewing industry. No hydration percentage appears in the sources reviewed.
flavor: Springy, thick-wavy flat noodle with soy-forward soup.
use: Served in clear shoyu soup in Kitakata shops.
craft: Resting after mixing is the step to ask the maker about; hydration was not quantified in available sources.

name: Kitakata asa-ra (morning ramen)
text: Custom of eating ramen early in the morning in Kitakata. One explanation is that workers coming off night shifts stopped at ramen shops, though this is given only as one account. Shop counts vary between sources, from about 120 shops for roughly 50,000 people to over 100 shops for roughly 40,000.
flavor: Light soy soup suited to morning.
use: Morning service at opening hours.
craft: Treat the origin as a theory; shop counts and population differ by source.

name: Nagaoka ginger shoyu ramen
ja: 長岡生姜醤油ラーメン
text: One of the five major Niigata ramen styles, born in snowy Nagaoka as a warming bowl. A pork-bone based, oil-rich soup with a large amount of ginger added to shoyu ramen.
flavor: Ginger-warming shoyu with a rich, oily soup.
use: Winter warming bowl.
craft: Ginger is dosed generously; the balance of ginger against pork-bone oil is the point. Specific ratios are not given in sources.
src: Niigata Kanko Navi: five major ramen
JR East Media: Niigata five major ramen

name: Niigata nogo miso ramen
ja: 新潟濃厚味噌ラーメン
text: One of the five major Niigata styles. Characteristically served with a separate dilution soup of bonito dashi or bone stock so the customer can adjust the strength of the thick miso soup.
flavor: Very thick miso soup, adjustable.
use: Diluted with the extra soup at the table.
craft: The warari soup is the distinctive service element; it must be hot enough not to cool the bowl.
src: Niigata Kanko Navi: five major ramen
JR East Media: Niigata five major ramen

name: Niigata assari shoyu ramen
ja: 新潟あっさり醤油ラーメン
text: A light shoyu ramen with niboshi-driven clear soup. Origin is attributed to the Nishibori area in Niigata city's Chuo ward, tied to a line of street stalls along the moat, though origin accounts are not settled. Sanyoshiya Honten is named as a representative shop.
flavor: Clean, niboshi-forward soy soup.
use: Standard light bowl of Niigata city.
craft: Niboshi quality and extraction time determine bitterness; accounts of the origin differ.
src: Niigata Kanko Navi: five major ramen

name: Sanjo curry ramen
text: One of the five major Niigata ramen. Said to have spread from curry-flavoured ramen served at a Sanjo canteen. The soup is mostly Japanese dashi with curry powder dissolved in, and each shop has its own character. The origin is not settled; sources also note that some tourism sites list a different fifth style.
flavor: Dashi-based curry soup.
use: Local specialty of Sanjo.
craft: Roux versus powder, and dashi balance vary per shop; origin accounts differ.
src: Niigata Kanko Navi: five major ramen

name: Koshu Hanten (Tsubame seabura origin shop, reported)
text: Tsubame ramen shop reported as the origin shop of Tsubame seabura ramen. Seabura ramen arose in Tsubame, a cutlery town, where many bowls were delivered to factories; thick noodle that resists stretching and a back-fat layer to keep the soup hot were adopted. A source names founder Xu Changxing (徐昌星) as the designer, but this is stated only as one account.
flavor: Back-fat-covered soy soup over very thick noodle.
use: Reference shop for seabura style.
craft: Back fat acts as a heat lid; the thick noodle was chosen for delivery.
src: Niigata Kanko Navi: five major ramen

name: Aotake-uchi (green-bamboo noodle pressing)
text: Noodle technique of Sano ramen in which dough is pressed with a green bamboo pole. Sano ramen noodles are flat and curly, with many internal air bubbles, which makes them cook quickly while keeping bite. Meshi-tsu notes that Asakusa's Rairaiken also made noodles by aotake, and similar methods were used widely in the Meiji and Taisho periods.
flavor: Springy, quick-cooking flat curly noodle.
use: Used with light clear shoyu soup.
craft: Air bubbles in the dough shorten boiling; watch boil time. Hydration is not specified in sources.

name: Horaiken (Sano ramen stall origin)
text: One account says a Chinese cook introduced the green-bamboo noodle method in the Taisho era, and his apprentice Ogawa Risaburo opened the Horaiken stall in 1930 (Showa 5). The Shimotsuke Shimbun presents Horaiken as the oldest surviving shop; the sources differ in how they describe the origin.
flavor: Clear shoyu soup with flat curly noodle.
use: Legend-class Sano shop.
craft: Treat the 1930 date as one account.

name: Yoshimuraya (iekei origin shop)
text: Founded in September 1974 by Yoshimura Minoru in Shin-sugita, Isogo ward, Yokohama, reportedly moved to the area in front of Yokohama Station in 1998. He is said to have thought of mixing Kyushu pork bone with Tokyo soy. The bowl is tonkotsu-shoyu with chicken oil, thick noodle from Sakai Seimen, nori and spinach, with chashu.
flavor: Pork-bone shoyu soup with chicken oil, thick noodle.
use: Source of the iekei lineage.
craft: Details such as floor space and moving dates vary across sources.
src: Wikipedia JA: 家系ラーメン

name: Nishimachi Taiki (Toyama Black origin shop)
text: Shop in Nishimachi, Toyama regarded as the origin of Toyama Black. Wikipedia says the soup started as a strongly soy-seasoned bowl for salt replenishment of labourers in post-war reconstruction; the shop's own page dates Taiki's birth to Showa 22 (1947). Served with a heavy amount of coarsely ground black pepper, intended to be eaten with rice, though the main shop is reported not to offer rice.
flavor: Very salty soy soup with black pepper.
use: Eaten with rice at other branches.
craft: The saltiness is a design feature; Taiki Nezuka is described as its only noren-wake.
